newsitem.title: UK: British January inflation unchanged at 3.1 percent.
newsitem.headline: British January inflation unchanged at 3.1 percent.

text.p: Britain's underlying annual inflation rate was unchanged at 3.1 percent in January compared with the previous month and remained stubbornly above the government's 2.5 percent target.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Thursday that underlying inflation, excluding volatile mortgage interest payments, fell 0.2 percent from December but the annual rate remained unchanged.

Some independent economists said the figures supported the Bank of England's argument, rejected by Conservative finance minister Kenneth Clarke, that interest rates should be increased to prevent inflation heading higher in the next two years.
"This gives a little more credence to the Bank of England's view that we should see a small tightening in monetary policy in the near future," said Philip Uglow, an economist at Union Plc.

But the government, which is anxious not to raise rates in the run-up to a looming election as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons, said the figures showed inflation was under control.
"Serious commentators, including the Bank of England in their Inflation Report yesterday, expect inflation to fall back over the coming months," Treasury minister Angela Knight said in a statement.
"The strength of sterling and this week's excellent producer price figures show inflation remains under firm control."
The headline rate of inflation rose to 2.8 percent year-on-year in January from 2.5 percent in December.

"The rise in the all-items 12-month rate was largely attributable to housing costs, though there were also smaller upward effects from food prices, particularly those for seasonal food, and from motoring costs," the ONS said.
Downward pressure came from prices for fuel and light, household goods, clothing and footwear.
